lesson_title: Week-One Check (replaces the day 5 08:45 quiz): recall and recognition on days 1-4

questions.question_stem: A prosecutor says Bitcoin 'can't be hacked', so a victim's report of stolen bitcoin must be false. What is the most accurate correction?
questions.correct_answer: The cryptography is strong; thefts happen at the endpoints, wallets and exchanges.
incorrect_answers: Miners can rewrite any past payment, so a theft can be undone after a report.
The ledger stays editable until a theft is reported, then it is locked for good.
Every payment can be reversed on request, so stolen bitcoin is never truly lost.
questions.explanation: The slide's answer to 'It can't be hacked' is that the cryptography is strong while thefts occur at wallets and exchanges. Payments are not editable at will or reversible on request.

specific_source.reading: Four beliefs to correct when you brief

questions.question_stem: A briefing calls Bitcoin and Arbitrum 'trustless'. Which correction fits the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Trust moves to cryptography and consensus: miners not colluding, a sequencer.
incorrect_answers: The wallet holds all of the trust once a payment is sent to the network.
A hidden bank or certificate authority still approves every payment on chain.
Chains with sequencers or elected block producers hold no trust assumptions at all.
questions.explanation: Trust is the set of assumptions a system's security rests on. Distributed systems move it to cryptography, consensus rules and an honest-majority assumption, and where it sits differs by chain.

specific_source.reading: "Trustless" is wrong: the trust just moves

questions.question_stem: A merchant waits six confirmations before releasing goods. What does the number six mean on Bitcoin?
questions.correct_answer: Six is a convention; each block makes reversal less likely, never impossible.
incorrect_answers: After six blocks a payment is final and no attacker of any size can ever reverse it.
Six is the protocol's finality rule, and nodes refuse chains that undo such blocks.
Six means six different nodes have each independently signed off on the payment.
questions.explanation: The slide calls six somewhat arbitrary. An attacker with under half the mining power sees the chance of catching up fall with each block, but never to zero.

questions.question_stem: An analyst holds the SHA-256 digest of a password. Why can a four-digit PIN be recovered from its digest but a long random string cannot?
questions.correct_answer: Nobody can reverse a hash; a PIN is a small set an attacker can hash in full.
incorrect_answers: Hash functions keep a copy of short inputs and give them back on request.
Short inputs make weaker digests that a simple calculation can then reverse.
Digests of long inputs are encrypted, while short-input digests are left bare.
questions.explanation: Pre-image resistance means the only way back is to guess inputs and hash each one. That works only when the input came from a small, guessable set.

specific_source.reading: You cannot run a hash backwards, only guess

questions.question_stem: A transaction paying Bob is broadcast. Before it is mined, a second transaction spending the same input and paying Carol, with a higher fee, is also broadcast. Which one does the trace follow?
questions.correct_answer: The version that is mined, since both spend the same inputs and only one can be.
incorrect_answers: The first one broadcast, since it is the real payment and the other is invalid.
Both versions, since the input funds two payments until a block settles them.
Neither, since every node always drops a transaction when it is replaced.
questions.explanation: Both versions spend the same inputs, so at most one can be mined. An unconfirmed payment can change, and the trace follows what the chain recorded.

questions.question_stem: A trace backwards from a deposit ends at a block's first transaction, which has no inputs from earlier outputs. What has the analyst reached?
questions.correct_answer: Newly mined coins from a block's coinbase, not someone's earlier payment.
incorrect_answers: An exchange's hot wallet, since only exchanges make transactions with no inputs.
A pool payout, since a mining pool pays its members in one transaction.
A burned output, which destroys the coins and ends the trace for good.
questions.explanation: New bitcoin enters only through the coinbase, the block's first transaction, which collects the subsidy and the fees.

specific_source.reading: Coinbase pays the miner: subsidy plus fees

questions.question_stem: An agent restores a seized 12-word seed phrase and the wallet is empty. Which explanation is consistent with how seed phrases work?
questions.correct_answer: A passphrase may be used; only the right one opens the funded wallet.
incorrect_answers: The words are only a hint; funds come back only from the original device.
The phrase expired once the wallet that made it was shut down for good.
The words must be re-entered in a different order for every new address.
questions.explanation: An optional passphrase changes the seed, so a phrase that opens an empty wallet may need its passphrase, or a wallet that reads its address type.

specific_source.reading: A seed phrase is the whole wallet as words

questions.question_stem: A subject uses a lightweight wallet that asks a public server about its addresses. What can that server learn?
questions.correct_answer: That the addresses likely belong to one entity, and the requests' IP address.
incorrect_answers: The wallet's private keys, because the server must sign every single reply it sends.
Nothing at all, because the wallet encrypts every address it sends out.
The subject's legal name, which the wallet supplies when it connects to it.
questions.explanation: Electrum never sends private keys, but a server sent many addresses can reasonably guess they belong to one entity, and it sees the client's IP address.

specific_source.reading: Servers learn which addresses a wallet has

questions.question_stem: A contract needs an asset's current price. Why can it not simply look the price up on a website?
questions.correct_answer: Every node must reach the same result, so outside data arrives via an oracle.
incorrect_answers: Validator nodes are barred from contacting any website over the internet.
Prices change too slowly for the chain to record and keep them current.
Contract languages have no way to store or compare numbers such as prices.
questions.explanation: Because every node must compute identical state changes, a contract has no network and no outside data of its own. An oracle puts outside data on chain and adds trust in its source.

specific_source.reading: A contract sees only what is on chain

questions.question_stem: A token transfer on Ethereum runs through the token's contract. Where does the transaction receipt show the tokens that moved?
questions.correct_answer: In the logs, as a Transfer event, not in the transaction's value field.
incorrect_answers: In the value field, as the token amount sent on to the receiving address.
In the gasUsed field, which counts the tokens moved with the fee.
In the contractAddress field, naming the new holder of the tokens.
questions.explanation: Token transfers show up in a receipt's logs, not in the transaction's value, which carries ETH. The analyst reads the logs the token contract emitted.

specific_source.reading: The receipt says what actually happened

questions.question_stem: An analyst compares ETH with a token on Ethereum. Which statement is accurate?
questions.correct_answer: ETH sits in Ethereum's own ledger; a token is a balance a contract keeps.
incorrect_answers: Both are balances kept by one shared contract that differs only in its name.
A token lives in the wallet's software and reaches the chain only if sold.
ETH is a token like any other, so its contract controls any freeze.
questions.explanation: A token is a balance the token's contract keeps, and its code decides who can create, move or freeze it. So the analyst reads the contract as well as the transaction.

specific_source.reading: A token is a balance a contract keeps

questions.question_stem: Which stablecoin type has an issuer that holds reserves behind the tokens and can freeze them in its contract's code?
questions.correct_answer: Fiat-backed coins such as USDT or USDC, where the issuer controls the contract.
incorrect_answers: Crypto-backed coins, because other crypto always backs a freeze function in code.
Algorithmic ones, because the algorithm freezes any address that sells under $1.
None of them, because nobody can stop a token once it is on a public blockchain.
questions.explanation: The type decides who stands behind the dollar. A fiat-backed issuer controls its contract; crypto-backed and algorithmic coins can be frozen only if their contract has a freeze function. (Issuer freeze powers as of Oct 2026.)

specific_source.reading: Three ways a stablecoin holds its peg

questions.question_stem: A transaction was submitted, then replaced by one with the same nonce and a higher fee. Where does the first version appear on the chain?
questions.correct_answer: Nowhere; the chain keeps only what was included, so the replaced one leaves no record.
incorrect_answers: In the block's logs, flagged as a replaced transaction occupying the same slot.
In the replacement's receipt, which lists the hash of the original it replaced.
In the next block, marked as failed, with its fee still charged to the sender.
questions.explanation: Pending transactions sit in each node's own mempool. One that is replaced or dropped leaves no on-chain record.

specific_source.reading: The mempool is public, so pending trades show

questions.question_stem: A token's price multiplied by a subject's 1,000,000 tokens gives 200 ETH, but the only pool holds 10 ETH. What does selling everything return?
questions.correct_answer: About 9.52 ETH: the quoted price fits tiny trades; the pool holds only 10 ETH.
incorrect_answers: About 200 ETH, because the quoted price is the price every sale receives.
About 100 ETH, because a pool never pays out more than half of its holdings.
About 10 ETH, the whole of the pool's ETH reserve, since a sale can empty the pool.
questions.explanation: Quoted value is not what can be sold. The pool's reserves are the limit, so the whole sale returns under 5% of the quoted figure.

specific_source.reading: Quoted value is not what can be sold

questions.question_stem: A withdrawal from an optimistic rollup reaches Ethereum about a week after it started, but a ZK rollup's waits only for a proof. Why?
questions.correct_answer: An optimistic rollup waits out a challenge window; a ZK one waits for its proof.
incorrect_answers: Optimistic rollups hold withdrawals during a weekly offline sequencer update window.
ZK rollups run on faster hardware, so their withdrawals are always quick.
Ethereum allows only one optimistic rollup withdrawal to land each week.
questions.explanation: The optimistic challenge window lets anyone submit a fraud proof. A ZK rollup's state change is finalized once its validity proof is accepted, with no challenge period. The challenge period is roughly seven days as of the 2026 lesson.

specific_source.reading: Optimistic waits a week; ZK waits for a proof

questions.question_stem: A lock-and-mint bridge moves value from chain A to chain B. Where does the analyst find the evidence?
questions.correct_answer: The lock on chain A and the matching mint of a copy on chain B.
incorrect_answers: One transaction on chain B showing the original coin arriving there.
A relayer's payment on chain B with no transaction on chain A at all.
A single message on chain A, since chain B keeps no record of it.
questions.explanation: Coins cannot leave their own chain. A lock-and-mint bridge locks or burns the coin on A and mints a copy on B, so the evidence sits on both chains.

specific_source.reading: A bridge moves a claim, not the coin
